title: Decode a practical-learning composition prompt
instructions: Read this original practice prompt, then answer all six task-analysis questions. Prompt: The ASEAN Youth Learning Blog asks students to share practical lessons. Write an article for secondary-school readers about one skill or idea you learned at school. Explain how you have used it, or could use it, in a different area of your life. Support your response with a specific example.

parts.prompt: What is the precise topic of the composition?

options.text: Why all school subjects are useful
One skill or idea learned at school
How youth blogs should be designed
The education systems of ASEAN countries

choice_rationales.A: The prompt narrows the topic to one skill or idea rather than the value of education in general.
choice_rationales.B: This preserves both the school-learning boundary and the one-focus limit.
choice_rationales.C: The blog supplies the situation and audience; its design is not the subject.
choice_rationales.D: ASEAN appears in the fictional blog name but the prompt does not ask for a comparison of education systems.

parts.hint: Ignore the setting words and identify the noun phrase that the response must develop.
parts.correct_explanation: The response must focus on one skill or idea that the writer learned at school.

parts.prompt: What is the main command, or thinking job?

options.text: List as many school lessons as possible
Argue that classroom learning is better than practical learning
Explain how the selected learning applies in another area of life
Describe the blog and its readers

choice_rationales.A: The prompt requests one focus and explanation, not a list.
choice_rationales.B: No comparison or argumentative position is required.
choice_rationales.C: The verb ‘explain’ requires the writer to show how the learning connects to a different area of life.
choice_rationales.D: The blog and readers establish the writing situation rather than the main content.

parts.hint: Find the instruction verb and ask what relationship it requires you to show.
parts.correct_explanation: The central job is to explain an application of the chosen learning beyond its original school setting.

options.text: Only the writer’s teachers
Secondary-school readers of a youth learning blog
University researchers
Young children learning to read

choice_rationales.A: A teacher may assess the work, but the prompt names blog readers as its intended audience.
choice_rationales.B: The writing situation explicitly identifies secondary-school readers of the youth blog.
choice_rationales.C: The prompt does not name an academic research audience.
choice_rationales.D: Secondary-school readers are older than beginning readers.

parts.hint: Look for the people named after the words ‘for’ or ‘to’ in the writing situation.
parts.correct_explanation: The article is addressed to secondary-school readers of the ASEAN Youth Learning Blog.

parts.prompt: Which THREE details are required by the scope of the prompt?

options.text: Focus on one school-learned skill or idea.
Compare learning from at least three school subjects.
Connect the learning to a different area of life.
Support the explanation with a specific example.
Prove that the application produced a major success.

choice_rationales.A: The word ‘one’ sets a clear content limit.
choice_rationales.B: The prompt narrows rather than multiplies the school learning to discuss.
choice_rationales.C: Application outside the original school context is central to the task.
choice_rationales.D: The final sentence explicitly requires a specific example.
choice_rationales.E: The example may show a use or possible use; a major successful result is not required.

parts.hint: Select only details stated as obligations, not optional ways to make the article impressive.
parts.correct_explanation: The response must keep one school-learned focus, apply it in another area of life and include a specific example.

parts.prompt: What satisfies the prompt’s personal-application requirement?

options.text: A dictionary definition of the skill only
A general claim that every student needs the skill
A list of school lessons with no situation outside class
A specific actual use or a realistic situation in which the writer could use the skill

choice_rationales.A: A definition explains meaning but does not apply the learning to the writer’s life.
choice_rationales.B: A claim about all students avoids the required personal connection.
choice_rationales.C: The prompt requires transfer to a different area of life.
choice_rationales.D: The wording ‘have used it, or could use it’ allows either an actual experience or a realistic future application.

parts.hint: Preserve both alternatives in ‘have used’ and ‘could use’.
parts.correct_explanation: The writer can use a real past experience or a credible future scenario, provided it is specific and outside the original classroom context.

parts.prompt: Which task contract best restates all essential requirements?

options.text: I will tell students everything I remember learning at school.
I will explain to secondary-school readers how one school-learned skill or idea applies in another area of life, using a specific actual or realistic example.
I will argue to teachers that practical skills should replace academic subjects.
I will describe one enjoyable school day and mention a blog at the end.

choice_rationales.A: This ignores the one-focus scope, application and specific-example requirements.
choice_rationales.B: This sentence preserves the topic, command, audience, scope and personal application.
choice_rationales.C: This changes both the audience and the command into an argument that was not requested.
choice_rationales.D: A school-day narrative does not necessarily explain transfer of learning to another area of life.

parts.hint: Choose the sentence that preserves every T-C-A-S-P feature without adding a new argument.
parts.correct_explanation: The complete contract identifies the reader, one school-learned focus, the explanatory job, transfer beyond school and a specific actual or realistic example.
